questions.question: In a trusted-setup proving system, what does “toxic waste” mean?
options: A secret trapdoor from setup that must be destroyed
The public proving key that must be kept private
The witness used by the prover that must be deleted
The transcript of the ceremony that must be hidden
questions.explanation: Toxic waste is the secret randomness (trapdoor) used during setup; if it leaks, soundness can fail.

questions.question: What does “universal setup” mean in most SNARK/SRS discussions?
options: One setup can support many circuits up to a size bound
The setup uses only public randomness so there is no secret
The prover never needs a proving key
The verifier must download the whole circuit each time
questions.explanation: Universal means reusable across many circuits (within a bound). It does not necessarily mean transparent.

questions.question: Why does leaking the setup trapdoor (e.g., τ) endanger soundness in KZG-like commitments?
options: It lets an attacker forge openings/proofs for false evaluations
It only reveals the committed polynomial but proofs stay valid
It only increases prover time but does not change security
It forces the verifier to do linear work in the polynomial size
questions.explanation: Knowing τ often lets an attacker compute proofs that satisfy the verification equation even when the claimed value is false.

questions.question: If you have a universal SRS with degree bound D, what does trimming to a smaller bound d do?
options: Keeps only the first d+1 powers and supports degree ≤ d polynomials
Re-runs a new trusted setup with a fresh secret τ
Turns the system into a transparent setup (no toxic waste)
Changes the field modulus used by the scheme
questions.explanation: Trimming derives per-circuit parameters from the universal SRS without introducing new toxic waste.

questions.question: In an updatable (multi-party) Powers-of-Tau-style ceremony, what is the key trust assumption?
options: At least one contributor is honest and deletes their secret
Every contributor must be honest or soundness fails
The verifier must know the final τ to verify proofs
The proving key must be kept secret forever
questions.explanation: Updatability aims for a 1-of-N trust model: one honest contribution is enough to keep τ unknown.

questions.question: In this lesson’s toy code, which computation captures the toxic-waste forgery idea?
options: Compute (C / g^y_fake)^(1/(τ - x)) to synthesize a proof
Hash the transcript to get a Fiat–Shamir challenge
Recompute the commitment by evaluating the polynomial at x
Encrypt the witness and send it to the verifier
questions.explanation: If τ is known, you can algebraically solve for a proof that makes the pairing check pass for an arbitrary y_fake.

questions.question: What is an operational drawback of circuit-specific setup?
options: Any circuit change can require regenerating setup-derived keys
Proof verification becomes linear in circuit size by definition
The system becomes post-quantum secure automatically
It prevents any form of parameter versioning
questions.explanation: Circuit-specific parameters are tied to one circuit; changing the circuit typically forces regeneration and careful migration.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes “universal” vs “transparent” setup?
options: Universal is about reuse across circuits; transparent is about having no secret trapdoor
Universal means no secret trapdoor; transparent means reuse across circuits
Universal means smaller proofs; transparent means larger proofs
Universal means Groth16; transparent means PLONK
questions.explanation: Universal concerns reusability (often still trusted). Transparent concerns parameter generation from public randomness (no toxic waste).
